Quick Read

Intel's data center revenue jumped 78% to $7 billion, yet the stock still plunged 50% in a month on weak guidance and cash burn.

NVIDIA invested $5 billion in Intel and chose its CPU for the DGX Rubin NVL8, while Oracle signed a multiyear Xeon deal.

CFO David Zinsner said, "I don't think this will be a year in which we see positive cash flow," as foundry losses persist.

Read More: Learn 7 ways to generate income with a $1,000,000+ portfolio (sponsor)

Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) trades at $56.28. The shares trade modestly above where they traded eight years ago, but the business underlying has been rebuilt around data center demand. Over the past month the stock fell 50.25%, and that drop came right after Intel posted its strongest data center growth in 15 years.

DaveAlan / iStock Unreleased via Getty Images
INTC Price Target — 24/7 Wall St.

Intel designs and manufactures semiconductors through two arms, Intel Products and Intel Foundry. In 2018 its fortunes rested on x86 chips for PCs and servers. Since then, Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD) has taken market share, and Arm-based processors and AI accelerators have challenged the traditional CPU market . On an adjusted basis, the stock has gained just 33.47% over eight years.

The latest drop followed third-quarter results that combined record server growth with a soft fourth-quarter outlook, heavy spending plans and a deepening PC slump .

Server CPU Demand Is Outrunning Intel's Supply

Data Center and AI revenue rose 78% to $7.32 billion. Segment operating income climbed to $3.04 billion from $964 million. Total revenue rose 20.9% to $16.51 billion, and non-GAAP EPS of $0.52 beat the $0.40 estimate. Management says demand "continues to meaningfully exceed available supply" and expects the industry to stay supply-constrained through 2027 and into 2028.

The AI expansion story extends well beyond the chip designers themselves (we covered seven suppliers powering, cooling and networking these data centers in a free report). Credo Just Dropped 32% in a Week. Is It Time to Sell, or Load Up? ©@Tiero via Canva, @Funtap from Getty Images via Canva
Key Takeaways

Credo shares fell 32% in the week through Nov. 5 in an AI hardware selloff, and Astera Labs and Marvell fell even further.

Credo had no bad news of its own, and its one announcement, with Oracle, was a small win in optics.

Analysts expect Credo's normalized EPS to nearly triple from fiscal 2026 to fiscal 2028, yet its forward P/E hit a three-year low.

The selling looks overdone, and Credo's early-December report will show whether its growth outlook still holds.

Credo Technology (CRDO:NASDAQ) stock fell 32% in the week through Nov. 5, with no bad news of its own, before bouncing 7% on Nov. 6. Its closest rivals had it even worse: Astera Labs (ALAB:NASDAQ) and Marvell Technology (MRVL:NASDAQ) fell harder as the Nasdaq 100 dropped 9%.

Washington did most of the damage

Most of the drop came after the Nov. 3 midterms. Democrats won both chambers of Congress and key governors' races, and several winners campaigned on tougher limits on building data centers. Texas, whose new governor-elect promised an immediate data-center moratorium, is the AI trade's "biggest worry," according to Yorkville Ives & Co.'s Dan Ives.

Intel's weak fourth-quarter outlook, issued after the close on Oct. 29, had already hit chip stocks on Oct. 30.

Astera Labs and Marvell fell even harder

Astera Labs is down 38%, even though it reported record third-quarter revenue of $584.9 million on Nov. 3, up 154% from a year earlier, and guided fourth-quarter revenue to $730 million to $750 million.

Marvell, down 39%, agreed on Nov. 2 to buy Lumentum in an all-stock deal valuing it at $115 billion, betting that optical links will replace copper. So what happens to Credo's copper cables, which drove over 99% of its revenue growth in fiscal 2026?

But Credo has its own optical push: management expects more than $600 million of optical revenue in fiscal 2027. And on Nov. 4, Credo and Oracle said the Open Compute Project had approved two optical telemetry specifications from a workstream the two companies lead. A small win, but in the right direction.

Quick Read

Five Walton heirs have added $100 billion to their fortunes in 2026, roughly what Oracle's Larry Ellison lost, despite never founding or running a company.

Walmart's stock has climbed 13% this year, outpacing the S&P 500 and dodging the AI sell-off, lifting its market value to $1 trillion.

Alice, Jim, and Rob Walton each gained $28 billion to reach $155 billion, a windfall the author attributes to luck.

Read More: Learn 7 ways to generate income with a $1,000,000+ portfolio (sponsor)

One could say the Walton family does not deserve to be rich. Among the world's wealthiest people, they are the only ones who did not start or serve as senior management of a company, most of which are in the tech industry. Nevertheless, five of Walmart (NYSE: WMT) founder Sam Walton's children and grandchildren have watched their combined net worth rise by $100 billion so far in 2026, Bloomberg reports. That is about the amount Oracle (NASDAQ: ORCL) founder Larry Ellison has lost in the same period.

Sam Walton started Walmart in 1942, at the age of 44. According to the Fortune 500, it was America's largest company for several years, until it yielded that position to Amazon (NASDAQ: AMZN) last year.

Niloo138 / iStock Editorial via Getty Images

Walmart remains a juggernaut. It employs 2.1 million people ("associates" as the company calls them). In the US, the figure is 1.6 million. Its footprint in its home market is 4,600 Walmart stores and 600 Sam's Club locations. Ninety percent of the US population lives within 10 miles of a Sam's Club or Walmart location.

In the most recent quarter, Walmart revenue rose 5.9% to $187.9 billion. Operating income rose 2.9% to $9.4 billion. John Furner, Walmart's President and CEO, said, "Our team delivered another good quarter, and we continue to make steady progress on the long-term value drivers of our business. Our multi-year growth in eCommerce is evidence that customers are choosing Walmart because we deliver price, speed, and convenience
across a broad assortment. At Walmart, they can have it all."

Cerebras Sinks 18% in a Week, CoreWeave Down 16% as AI Stocks Slide: Buy Before Earnings? ©panumas nikhomkhai from Pexels, Vladimir_Timofeev from Getty Images via Canva
Key Takeaways

Cerebras shares fell 18% in a week as AI stocks sold off on Oracle's $20 billion raise and again after the midterms.

Cerebras made no announcement of its own, and CoreWeave and Oracle fell on the same AI worries.

Analysts expect revenue to more than triple next year, and the stock's forward sales multiple has fallen far from its June peak.

The third-quarter report and the IPO lockup's end come close together, so waiting for the numbers makes more sense.

Cerebras Systems (CBRS:NASDAQ) stock is down 18% in the past week without any news of its own. The AI trade sold off twice, taking CoreWeave (CRWV:NASDAQ) and Oracle (ORCL:NYSE), its newest cloud partner, down too.

Oracle's $20 billion bill landed on its partners

Oracle agreed on Oct. 27 to offer Cerebras's inference on its cloud. Before Monday's open, Oracle filed to raise $20 billion in stock and bonds for its AI buildout. AI infrastructure stocks slid, and Oracle fell 11% over the week. UBS cut its target to $250 from $330 that morning but kept a Buy, so the cut doesn't explain the drop. For now, the deal is more liability than help. It's too new to show up in revenue, yet the stock already trades on how Oracle funds its data centers.

Thursday's rout hit every data-center name

On Thursday, chip and AI stocks sank on fears the Democrats' midterm sweep will tighten AI rules and slow new data centers. The Nasdaq Composite fell 6%, and the Philadelphia chip index 12%. CoreWeave's growth depends on new data centers just as Cerebras's does, and it's down 16% in the past week. It ended June with about $104 billion in revenue backlog. Its next report will show whether that fear reaches customers' orders.

The report and the lockup come first

Analysts expect revenue of $890 million this year, then $2.96 billion in 2027 and $7.54 billion in 2028.

And the stock is far cheaper on them than after its May IPO.

Cerebras Systems (CBRS): forward (NTM) price/sales, since it listed (TIKR)

At 13x forward sales as of Thursday, it trades well below its 36x average since listing and June's 63x peak. Analysts' average target is still $275, about three times Friday's close.

Two risks still hang over the stock. Culper Research announced a short on Oct. 28, claiming "$CBRS wafers break down after just ~2 years." The IPO lockup on early holders' shares also ends soon. Under Cerebras's 10-Q, it ends two trading days after the Nov. 12 third-quarter report, or sooner at the 180-day mark. That mark falls early next week, before the report.
